answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type for an account/cluster: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (API for MongoDB is created as a databaseAccount with kind or capabilities set to MongoDB).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the core CLI group az cosmosdb. Example to create a Mongo-compatible account: az cosmosdb create -g MyRG -n my-docdb-account --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=eastus --default-consistency-level Session

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep/ARM: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (e.g. resource cosmos 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15' = { name: 'acct' ... }). Terraform (AzureRM): resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "example" { name = "acct" location = azurerm_resource_group.rg.location offer_type = "Standard" kind = "MongoDB" ... }  (Note: newer dedicated MongoDB cluster features may expose additional resources in the provider, but the standard resource is azurerm_cosmosdb_account.)

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer:
Typical Cosmos DB (Mongo API) connection string looks like:
mongodb://<USERNAME>:<PASSWORD>@<ACCOUNT_NAME>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&authSource=admin&appName=@<ACCOUNT_NAME>@
Notes: scheme is mongodb:// (mongodb+srv is not always supported for Cosmos accounts); host suffix is <account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com; TLS port commonly 10255 for the Cosmos-hosted Mongo endpoint; options must include ssl=true (or tls=true), replicaSet=globaldb, retryWrites=false, and authSource=admin for SCRAM creds.

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Cosmos DB supports multiple billing models: the classic model is RU/s (provisioned throughput or autoscale RUs) or serverless (RU consumption billed per request). For Mongo-compatible workloads you can also choose dedicated vCore-based MongoDB clusters (instance tiers like M10/M30 in the managed Mongo offering) — those are billed by compute (vCore/instance size) and storage. So depending on account type you will see RU/s (for Cosmos accounts) or vCore/instance pricing for dedicated MongoDB clusters.

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: Primary auth for the MongoDB API is Mongo-style credentials (SCRAM username/password created for the account) and the account keys for Cosmos control-plane. Cosmos also supports Cosmos resource tokens and Azure RBAC/Azure AD role-based access for some data-plane APIs (primarily the native Cosmos SDKs/SQL API). For typical Mongo drivers you authenticate with the SCRAM credentials in the connection string. Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) authentication is supported for Cosmos DB data-plane via the Azure SDKs (azure-cosmos) by acquiring an AAD token (scope https://cosmos.azure.com/.default) and using it with the SDK; AAD-based auth is not generally available for raw MongoDB drivers in the same way — for Mongo API you should use SCRAM creds. (If you need AAD, use the Azure SDKs or a supported dedicated-cluster option that advertises AAD integration.)

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: For MongoDB-compatible workloads use the official MongoDB drivers (e.g., pymongo/motor for Python) so existing MongoDB code (and ODMs like Beanie) works. There is a separate azure-cosmos SDK but that targets Cosmos DB's SQL/core API and is not the right choice for Mongo wire-protocol workloads.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Full-text for Cosmos DB is normally done with Azure Cognitive Search (indexing data from Cosmos DB), or by using text indexes in the MongoDB API for simple text queries. Hybrid (vector + text) search is typically implemented by either: 1) using a vector-capable search engine that supports hybrid scoring (Azure Cognitive Search recently added vector search features), or 2) performing vector nearest-neighbour lookup using the vector index and then re-ranking/filtering candidates by text score in the application layer. Cosmos does not expose a Mongo-Atlas-style integrated Search UI; you typically integrate with Azure Cognitive Search or do application-side hybrid scoring.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Supported MongoDB wire protocol/server versions depend on the account configuration; historically Cosmos offered compatibility for MongoDB 3.6/3.4/4.0/4.2 and more recently newer clusters may advertise compatibility with 5.x or 6.x (and some managed offerings advertise 7.0). Commonly-missing or limited features vs a stock MongoDB server include server-side JavaScript ($where), some storage-engine and oplog management controls, full replica-set control, certain aggregation stages or newer pipeline operators (depending on version), and historically some limitations around multi-document transactions and change streams (behaviour depends on account type and supported wire version). Always verify the exact supported server version for your account before relying on newer MongoDB features.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer:
Options:
- Use the Azure Cosmos DB Emulator (mcr.microsoft.com/cosmosdb/linux/azure-cosmos-emulator or the Windows installer) for SQL API testing; the emulator exposes the SQL endpoints (not all APIs are supported for Mongo). Note: the emulator historically does NOT fully support the MongoDB wire protocol.
- For MongoAPI development, run a local MongoDB container, e.g. docker run -p 27017:27017 --name mongo mongo:7.0, and point your app at mongodb://localhost:27017. For testing Mongo-specific features rely on a local mongo image rather than the Cosmos emulator.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Support for change streams depends on the account and the MongoDB compatibility version. Some managed Mongo/Cosmos offerings support change streams (or an equivalent CDC feed) but earlier Cosmos Mongo API tiers did not; dedicated MongoDB cluster offerings are more likely to support change-stream semantics. If supported you may need to use a MongoDB server version compatibility that exposes change streams and ensure the account/cluster is created with that capability. (Check the account's supported features; there is no universal guarantee across all Cosmos Mongo API accounts.)

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: The documentdb-specific MCP server (named documentdb in the environment described) provides data-plane inspection and tools for DocumentDB/Cosmos DB. The general azure MCP server covers generic Azure resource management but the documentdb MCP server provides service-specific data-plane commands (collection/index inspection, query plans) that the sample expects.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Microsoft originally launched a document database service called Azure DocumentDB; that technology evolved into Azure Cosmos DB (DocumentDB was essentially the original name). Azure Cosmos DB is the platform that provides multiple APIs (SQL/core, MongoDB-compatible API, Cassandra, Gremlin, Table). This Azure DocumentDB name is the historic name for Cosmos DB and is not the same as any unrelated open-source project named DocumentDB.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Under the MongoDB API the service is an emulation layer on top of the Cosmos DB engine (Microsoft's storage/replication/query engine) or on a managed MongoDB engine for dedicated Mongo clusters. From application code you use the MongoDB driver and most Mongo operations work, but there are behavioral differences (index semantics, consistency models, transaction and aggregation edge-cases, and unsupported server-side features). Expect to test and validate any advanced MongoDB features against the chosen account type.

answers.question: Which database name will this sample use?
answers.answer: Use the database named sample_customer_360_20 for all sample collections and operations.

answers.question: How should the app read the cluster connection string at runtime?
answers.answer: Read the Mongo connection URI from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI (do not write the secret into files or repos). In Python: os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI'] and pass it to motor.motor_asyncio.AsyncIOMotorClient or pymongo.MongoClient.

answers.question: Which Python client stack will the sample use with Beanie ODM?
answers.answer: Use the standard MongoDB Python ecosystem: motor (asyncio driver) as the transport, pymongo-compatible URI, and Beanie ODM on top of motor. Example client creation: client = motor.motor_asyncio.AsyncIOMotorClient(os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']) then use Beanie.init_beanie(database=client['sample_customer_360_20'], document_models=[...]).

answers.question: What vector index definition will the sample create for embedding search?
answers.answer:
Create a vector index on the embedding field with HNSW parameters. Example Mongo shell command (adjust names/params to the cluster's exact index API):
db.profiles.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { vector: { dimensions: 1536, method: 'hnsw', metric: 'cosine', M: 16, efConstruction: 200 } })
(If the managed service requires different option names, translate to the provider-specific index creation call; the sample will attempt this command against the live cluster and record results.)

answers.question: What collections and indexes will the sample create?
answers.answer: Collections: profiles (holds input profiles and embeddings), golden_records (final merged profiles), audit_logs (audit entries for merges). Indexes: vector index on profiles.embedding, text index on profiles.name and profiles.bio (e.g. db.profiles.createIndex({ name: 'text', bio: 'text' })), and unique index on golden_records._id (default).
